sentence: Because the road ahead is narrower than the cell.
claim: A red cell is about 7.5 µm across, yet it passes microvessels only about 3 µm wide, so the vessels ahead of it can be narrower than the cell.
source_title: Red blood cells are highly deformable (University of Rochester, Biomedical Engineering)
note: Excerpt: highly deformable, 'which enables them to traverse microvessels whose diameter is only about 3µm'.

sentence: Meet a red blood cell: a dimpled disc, about seven micrometers across.
claim: Red blood cells are dimpled (biconcave) discs, 7–8 µm across.
note: Excerpt gives 7–8 µm and 'they lack a nucleus, organelles, and cannot divide'. Other texts give 7.5–8 µm; 'about seven' sits at the low end of the range. A scale pill, if one shows the size, reads 7.5 µm.

sentence: It even pushed out its own nucleus.
claim: A maturing mammalian red blood cell expels its nucleus (enucleation): a ring of actin pinches the nucleus off, and macrophages clear it, so mature red cells have none.
source_title: Whitehead Institute, How red blood cells nuke their nuclei
note: Rewritten 24 Oct with the script (v2). The biconcave shape moved into c2.

sentence: You have about twenty-five trillion of them: most of your own cells.
claim: A reference adult has about 30 trillion human cells, about 84% of them red blood cells (about 25 trillion). The body also holds about 38 trillion bacteria, hence 'your own cells'.
source_title: BioNumbers 113005: distribution of cell number and mass by cell type (Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016, PLOS Biology)
note: Cross-check fix applied: 'most of the cells in your body' was false once bacteria count. The 84% share is from BioNumbers' excerpt of the paper's figure and Medical News Today; 0.84 × 30 trillion = 25.2 trillion (computed).

sentence: Follow it as the vessel branches, and branches again, into a capillary.
claim: Arteries branch into smaller vessels, the arterioles, which feed capillary beds.
source_title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, chapter 20 review (LibreTexts copy)
note: Excerpt: 'Arteries transport blood away from the heart and branch into smaller vessels, forming arterioles. Arterioles distribute blood to capillary beds, the sites of exchange with the body tissues.'

sentence: There's no room to overtake, so cells go through in single file.
claim: The narrowest microvessels (about 3 µm) are smaller than a red cell, and in capillaries red cells travel in single file.
source_title: Red blood cells are highly deformable (University of Rochester, Biomedical Engineering)
note: Excerpt: 'in capillaries, red blood cells travel in single file separated by plasma gaps'.

claim: Squeezing through narrow capillaries, a red cell deforms at constant volume and nearly constant surface area: its membrane strongly resists stretching.
source_title: Halpern & Secomb 1989, The squeezing of red blood cells through capillaries with near-minimal diameters, J. Fluid Mech. 203:381
note: The membrane strongly resists stretching: a squeezed red cell keeps nearly constant surface area, so it folds rather than stretches (the wrong guess the line sets up).

sentence: The dimples give it spare surface for its volume, so it folds into a parachute instead.
claim: A red cell's surface-area-to-volume ratio, more than its stiffness, decides how narrow a passage it can get through.
source_title: Namvar et al. 2020, Surface area-to-volume ratio, not cellular rigidity, determines red blood cell traversal through small capillaries (bioRxiv)
note: 'Spare surface for its volume' is the standard reading of that ratio (a sphere of the same volume has less surface). Preprint; the cross-check also accepts it as the standard explanation.

sentence: The dimples give it spare surface for its volume, so it folds into a parachute instead.
claim: In capillary flow, a red cell changes from a disc to a parachute shape as the flow speeds up.
source_title: Noguchi & Gompper 2005, Shape transitions of fluid vesicles and red blood cells in capillary flows, PNAS 102:14159
note: Excerpt (PMC1242298 abstract): 'a model RBC is found to transit from a nonaxisymmetric discocyte to an axisymmetric parachute shape'. A simulation that the authors report agrees with experiments.

sentence: The tightest are about three micrometers: less than half its width.
claim: Red cells traverse microvessels only about 3 µm across, about 40% of a 7.5 µm cell.
source_title: Red blood cells are highly deformable (University of Rochester, Biomedical Engineering)
note: Cross-check fix: replaces the unsupported 'only about half its width' [S3, PMC8215585]. 3 / 7.5 = 0.40 (computed).

sentence: And it keeps squeezing through, all its life: about a hundred and twenty days.
claim: A red blood cell lives about 120 days on average.
source_title: Erythrocyte Aging, MeSH (US National Library of Medicine)
note: Excerpt: 'This limits the average life span of an erythrocyte to 120 days.'

sentence: Stiff sickle cells can jam the smallest vessels, where oxygen is handed out.
claim: Capillary beds are extremely narrow, which slows red cells and gives gas exchange time to happen.
source_title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology, 18.3 Erythrocytes (LibreTexts copy)
note: Excerpt: 'Capillary beds are extremely narrow, slowing the passage of the erythrocytes and providing an extended opportunity for gas exchange to occur.'

sentence: Meanwhile, as you watched, your bone marrow made over a hundred million new red cells.
claim: The body makes about two million red blood cells every second, in the bone marrow.
source_title: Blood cells (MedlinePlus, US National Library of Medicine)
note: Excerpt: 'The body makes about two million red blood cells every second!' The tally is 2,000,000 × t from frame 0; the line starts at about 59 s (about 118 million), and 'over a hundred million' holds for any start after 50 s (computed). Consistent with 25 trillion cells / 120 days = 2.4 million a second (computed).

sentence: Room for about a billion passengers.
claim: A red blood cell holds about 270 million hemoglobin molecules.
source_title: Hemoglobin and heme products (Merck technical article)
note: Excerpt: '~270 million hemoglobin molecules' per cell; Wikipedia's red blood cell article gives the same. The cross-check found 250–300 million across sources, so the product is 1.0–1.2 billion: 'about a billion' holds. 270 million × 4 = 1.08 billion (computed).

sentence: Room for about a billion passengers.
claim: Each hemoglobin has four heme groups, each binding one oxygen molecule: four O₂ per hemoglobin.
source_title: OpenStax Biology 2e, 39.4 Transport of Gases in Human Bodily Fluids
note: Excerpt: hemoglobin is 'made of four subunits'; 'each heme group that contains iron binds one oxygen molecule'.

sentence: Stiff sickle cells can jam the smallest vessels, where oxygen is handed out.
claim: In sickle cell disease, red cells with hemoglobin S form rigid strands and become sticky; in the smallest vessels they can get stuck and clog the capillaries, blocking blood flow.
source_title: NHLBI, Sickle Cell Disease fact sheet (July 2022)
note: Excerpt (NHLBI fact sheet PDF): 'some of them form into rigid strands and become sticky. Those strands often get stuck, clogging the capillaries.' MedlinePlus agrees. 'Can' keeps it to what the sources say; the cause is hemoglobin S, not the dimple, and the line doesn't say otherwise. A 2012 Drexel study places most obstruction just downstream of the capillaries; 'the smallest vessels' covers both. A physiologist signs off the wording and the naming; pin the NHLBI fact sheet in the comments if it stays.
